Play Nice but Win: A CEO’s Journey from Founder to Leader

Michael Dell and James Kaplan. Portfolio, $28 (336p) ISBN 978-0-593-08774-9

After spending much of the last decade engaged in a pitched battle to hold onto his eponymous computer company, a triumphant but bruised Dell ( Direct from Dell ) looks back at a lifetime of naysayers and relishes the chance to set the record straight in this intimate, insider portrait of a tech titan under siege. Chapters alternate between Dell narrating the ferocious battle to buy out the company and his transformation from a scrappy, entrepreneurial teen to a college-dorm dwelling CEO, two threads that are linked by his singular faith in the future of personal computing. Dell describes his aggressors: the “trouble-making opportunist” Carl Icahn, who waged a public war against Dell as the founder and CEO sought to take his company private and insulted Dell while he restrained from commenting on anything related to ongoing negotiations; shareholders who “abandoned” him during a spate of poor earnings; and a business media that had “an ax to grind.” While the personal narrative is fast-paced and

About the book

In 1984, Michael Dell was a University of Texas student about to drop out, hiding signs of his new PC business in the bathroom of his dorm room. Nearly three decades on, the founder and head of Dell Technologies was battling to save it. Written with James Kaplan, the memoir covers three battles: to launch the company, to keep it and to transform it. Dell recalls the mentors who helped him make a business of his passion, rivals who turned into friends, enemies or a mix of the two, and predators watching for weakness, and describes how he grew into the chief executive the company needed. It became a Wall Street Journal best seller.
Matthew McConaughey praised it as an autobiographical thriller with Michael Dell as its gangster protagonist, never seeking a fight yet relishing every brawl.
